stem.en: Kabir says the moong "could just fix its own nitrogen and not pay the bacteria". What would that cost?

text.en: The fixing enzyme is huge, is poisoned by oxygen, and spends about sixteen ATP per nitrogen molecule. A plant that ran it in its own cells would have to wall off oxygen-free rooms and spend a large share of its sugar. Paying a specialist that already does it is cheaper.

feedback.en: No plant does, in four hundred million years. The enzyme's demands are why.

text.en: The plant does not have nitrogen in it.

feedback.en: Every protein and every nucleotide in the plant has nitrogen. It needs a lot, and it cannot take it from the air.

text.en: The bacteria would attack the plant.

feedback.en: They are held inside cells the plant controls. The deal is stable because each side's cheating is caught, which is the arms-race lesson.

explanation.en: Weigh the costs. A hard reaction, an oxygen-hating enzyme, and a coin bill of sixteen per molecule. Outsourcing to a partner that lives on it is the cheaper route, and the legumes took it.
